Medicines outside direct price controls remain regulated through market monitoring and limits on annual price increases. A stable regulatory framework supports long-term investment in manufacturing, quality and research, while allowing government intervention where affordability concerns arise. Imagine a worker at a brick kiln in eastern Uttar Pradesh who is the sole wage-earner in a family of five. Although he earns enough to keep the household’s spending above the World Bank’s extreme poverty line of $3 per day, a look inside his house would show that his wife and children are underweight, the family cooks on a wood stove rather than on LPG, they share a latrine with neighbours and live under a thatched roof — all signs that we would associate with poverty. When we look closely, income-based poverty measures of the kind often reported miss a lot about the reality of people’s lives.
To address this concern, the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative and the United Nations Development Programme developed the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) that has been applied globally. Rather than focussing on income, the MPI looks at 10 indicators of health, education and living standards. The index works like a scorecard with 18 points.
Each of the four health and education indicators is worth three points, and each of the six living-standard indicators is worth one. A household that scores six or more is counted as poor. In the case of the family in UP, the family loses three points because the mother is underweight, and one point each for cooking fuel, sanitation and housing.
That makes six, exactly the poverty line, with any more deprivations exacerbating their poverty status. If the family is able to build a toilet with help from the government, its score would drop to five and it would be counted as having left poverty, even if the other deprivations are unchanged. The difference between a share's fair market value on the date of exercise and its exercise price is treated as a perquisite and taxed at rates of up to 39% for employees in the highest tax bracket. Consider an employee exercising 10,000 options at ₹100 when shares are worth Rs 1,000 makes a notional gain of Rs 90 lakh. Having paid Rs 10 lakh to acquire the shares, with no cash received, he could still face a tax bill of ~Rs 35 lakh on paper gain. The problem is worse in unlisted companies, where the Rs 1,000 valuation is based on a formula, not an actual market price. Employees are taxed on gains they may not be able to realise for years. Eligible startups can defer Esop tax until a specified triggering event, acknowledging liquidity crunch caused by taxing gains at exercise. Why should this relief stop at startups? If they owe tax of around 39% on the Rs 900 spread between the exercise price of Rs 100 and market price of Rs 1,000, they may have to sell nearly 40% of their shares immediately to meet the liability. This forces employees to sell part of their equity incentive before they choose to, potentially at a loss. Worse, any subsequent capital loss can be set off only against capital gains, not salary income. So, while notional Esop gain is taxed at slab rates, a loss on sale can't be offset against it. Science alone makes ethanol seem like an inefficient fuel. The conversion efficiency of sunlight-to-biomass-energy is a low percentage figure for sugarcane, compared to around 20% for sunlight-to-electricity through solar panels. And food security is sacrosanct.
The typical reason why a fuel is chosen is economics: People always want a cheaper alternative. But this isn’t always a sufficient driver. Energy security is another consideration.
A third factor, especially in the case of ethanol in India, is what we can call human-fiscal equilibrium. Even if ethanol doesn’t save us money, it changes the recipient of this money — from foreign sellers of oil to India’s farmers. These are the reasons why ethanol should remain on the table as a component of our energy portfolio.
More so, when it is in the form of vehicles capable of running on ethanol alone — the E100 category, for which the Centre has just released rules — which is distinct from a goal of 100%, economy-wide replacement of petroleum by ethanol. The conventional argument against ethanol is that it comes from sugarcane, but India must prioritise sugar for food rather than divert cane for ethanol production. There are three routes of ethanol production from sugarcane: One, from cane juice (which impacts sugar production), from B-heavy molasses (which marginally impacts sugar production), and from C-heavy, residual molasses (which doesn’t impact sugar production).
India has shifted ethanol production away from the first type based on national needs. Now, there is another aspect to the debate: the shift away from sugarcane to grains for ethanol production. In recent times, about two-thirds of India’s ethanol need for 20% blending with petroleum has come from grains.
This has involved fresh, fit-for-human-consumption grains and, crucially, reject-grains both. Grain-based ethanol production not only reduced dependence on sugarcane but also resolved the seasonality challenge of extraction from the cane crop. Thus, the diversity of inputs already partly mitigates the impact on food security.
Throw in technology-aided improvements in productivity and new farming techniques such as precision and vertical farming, and the pressures on land and food supply ease to a fair degree. New Delhi [India], October 30 (ANI): The government has formally notified the constitution of the National Social Security Board for Unorganised Workers and Gig and Platform Workers under the Code on Social Security, bringing workers in the digital platform economy within the country's statutory social security framework. The Board will recommend welfare schemes for different categories of unorganised workers, including gig and platform workers, and monitor the implementation of social welfare schemes administered by the Central Government. It will also advise the government on matters related to the administration of the Code on Social Security.
The Ministry of Labour and Employment described the notification as a "landmark step toward ensuring comprehensive social security for India's massive informal workforce".The Board will be chaired by the Union Minister for Labour and Employment and will include representatives from Central and State Governments, aggregator companies, employers, civil society organisations, workers' unions and associations representing gig and platform workers. The inclusion of aggregator companies and worker associations in the Board's composition provides representation to both sides of the platform-based work ecosystem in the body responsible for recommending and reviewing welfare measures. The Board will be required to meet at least three times a year and follow the rules of procedure prescribed by the Central Government for conducting its meetings.
Its responsibilities will include recommending suitable social security schemes for different sections of unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers, besides monitoring existing welfare schemes administered by the Centre. It will also review record-keeping functions carried out at the State level and examine expenditure from the relevant fund and account. The Central Government may assign additional functions to the Board from time to time.
The notification comes under the Code on Social Security, which provides the statutory framework for addressing social security requirements across different categories of workers. A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) in Bhutan has triggered concerns in India, with authorities issuing flood warnings in parts of Assam and West Bengal over a possible rise in the Sankosh River. Rescue and disaster response teams have been deployed in vulnerable areas as officials monitor the movement of floodwater.
The outburst was reported on Thursday evening at Shintaphu Lake, also known as Shintaphu Tsho, below Wakila Mountain in Bhutan’s Gasa district. The lake is located in the upper reaches of the Mo Chhu river basin, which forms part of the Punatsangchhu basin. The river is known as the Sankosh after entering India.
The flash flood partially damaged a solar-powered irrigation system in Dochhukha-Dzomlingthang-Ritsa Chiwog, under Guma Gewog in Punakha. The facility, installed earlier this year to address local water shortages, has stopped functioning. The full extent of the damage is yet to be assessed.
Floodwater also swept debris onto a section of the Punakha-Gasa Highway near Dzomlingthang. No casualties have been reported so far.
Shintaphu Lake is among Bhutan’s 17 glacial lakes identified as potentially dangerous. An official from the National Centre for Hydrology and Meteorology said a water-level monitoring station was operating at Taktsimakhang, but it had not triggered an alert when the initial reports emerged. The extent of the outburst and its impact downstream remained unclear.
The Centre issued an advisory warning of a possible sudden rise in the Sankosh River. West Bengal’s Alipurduar district and Assam’s Dhubri district are among the areas facing a potential threat.

The advisory warned that floodwater could reach the India-Bhutan border within six to eight hours. District authorities have been asked to monitor river levels and take necessary precautions.
Superintendent of Police Amit Kumar Shaw said around 4,000 to 5,000 people had been shifted to shelters set up in school buildings, while over 6,000 others had been relocated to safe areas. NEW DELHI: The Election Commission (EC) on Thursday extended the schedule for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in six states and Union Territories: Nagaland, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Maharashtra and Delhi. In Delhi, the deadline for filing claims and objections has been extended by 26 days, from October 30 to November 25. The period for issuing notices and disposing of claims and objections will now run until December 15, instead of November 30.
The final electoral roll will be published on December 22. The Commission acted on a request from the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) under the proviso to Rule 12 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The draft roll was published on August 31, with October 1, 2026, as the qualifying date.
In Andhra Pradesh and Haryana, the period for issuing notices and disposing of claims and objections has been extended until November 20, 2026, from the earlier deadline. The final electoral rolls in both states will be published on November 30, with July 1, 2026, as the qualifying date. The Commission’s letters to the CEOs of Andhra Pradesh and Haryana cited their requests dated October 29, 2026, and referred to earlier orders modifying the SIR schedule.
The EC has directed officials to inform all concerned about the revised schedule and give it wide publicity through available media. Political parties are also to be informed in writing. Copies of the letters have been sent to the chief secretaries.
